name: Montana

notes: Groceries aren't taxed; resort taxes don't apply to food bought unprepared.
Full-service restaurants and quick-service restaurants: restaurant food and drinks pay no state tax; resort communities and areas add 3% or 4%, counted where they apply year-round.

Liquor is sold through state agency stores at prices that include the state's 40.5% markup and excise and license taxes of up to 16% and 10% of the retail price (by the distiller's size); beer pays $1.30 to $4.30 a barrel and table wine 27 cents a liter. Left out here; drinks served in resort communities' bars and restaurants pay the resort tax, counted in the restaurant rate.

Cigarettes pay $1.70 a pack of 20, other tobacco 50% of the wholesale price, moist snuff 85 cents an ounce and premium cigars 50% of the wholesale price or 35 cents each, whichever is less; left out here.

Household supplies, pets and toys, personal care products, clothing, home furnishings, and auto parts: Montana has no sales tax on goods; in resort communities, luxuries sold to visitors pay the resort tax, which isn't counted here.
Barber and beauty services, laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: Montana doesn't tax these services.
Gasoline pays 33 cents a gallon and diesel 29.75 cents, left out here.

Montana has no general sales tax. Resort taxes of 3% or 4% apply year-round in Big Sky, Red Lodge, Whitefish, Columbia Falls, West Yellowstone, the Cooke City area (with Silver Gate) and St. Regis, and for part of the year in Virginia City, Craig, Gardiner and Wolf Creek; since 2025 voters may also spend the extra 1% on workforce housing (SB 172, HB 162).

Lodging pays the state's 8% (a 4% lodging facility use tax and a 4% sales tax) plus any resort tax, and car rentals 4%; adult-use marijuana pays 20% and medical marijuana 4% (MCA 15-64-102). Not counted here.
A 2025 bill to let local governments levy a tourism tax of up to 4% (HB 489) died in the legislature (as reported).
gaps: Montana has no state or local general sales tax.

Resort communities and resort areas levy a resort tax of up to 3%, plus up to 1% more for infrastructure or housing where voters approve it (MCA 7-6-1503), on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries. It is counted in the restaurant categories wherever it applies year-round: in the figures where the community or area holds at least half a census tract (Big Sky 4%, Red Lodge 4%, Whitefish 3%, Columbia Falls 3%), and named on the pages of West Yellowstone (4%), Cooke City and Silver Gate (3%) and St. Regis (3%), each under half of its tract. Seasonal taxes (Virginia City, Craig, Gardiner, Wolf Creek) and the Big Mountain and Red Lodge Mountain resort areas, which aren't Census places, are named on the pages they touch, not counted. Which goods count as luxuries is set locally, so the tax is not applied to the other categories.

Unincorporated resort areas (Big Sky, Cooke City, Craig, Gardiner, St. Regis, Wolf Creek) are recorded on the Census place of the same name (Cooke City's also on Silver Gate), whose boundary may differ from the resort area's.
Lodging pays the state's 8% (a 4% lodging facility use tax and a 4% sales tax) and car rentals 4% (MCA 15-65-111, 15-68-102); not counted here.

3006325: Big Sky's resort tax is 4% (3% plus 1% for infrastructure since July 1, 2020) on lodging, restaurants and bars, ski areas and other destination recreation, and luxuries in the Big Sky Resort Area District, which spans Gallatin and Madison counties and runs to 2032; it is counted in Big Sky's restaurant rate (Big Sky Resort Area District).
3016600: Columbia Falls' 3% resort tax on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries, collected since October 1, 2021 and running through September 30, 2040 (city code chapter 3.20), is counted in Columbia Falls' restaurant rate.
3017350: The Cooke City resort area, which also takes in Silver Gate, levies a 3% resort tax year-round on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); it would be counted in Cooke City's restaurant rate.
Cooke City is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3018025: The Craig resort area levies a 4% resort tax from April 1 to November 15 on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce; the Department of Revenue's list gives 3%); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
3029950: The Gardiner resort area levies a 4% resort tax from June 1 to September 30 on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
3061525: Red Lodge's resort tax is 4% (3% renewed by voters on June 2, 2020, plus 1% for stormwater projects since July 7, 2020) on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries; it is counted in Red Lodge's restaurant rate (City of Red Lodge; the Department of Commerce's map still shows 3%).
The Red Lodge Mountain resort area, the ski area west of the city, has levied a 2% resort tax since January 1, 2008 (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since the area isn't a Census place.
3065575: The St. Regis resort area levies a 3% resort tax year-round on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); it would be counted in St. Regis' restaurant rate.
St. Regis is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3068425: Silver Gate is in the Cooke City resort area, which levies a 3% resort tax year-round on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); it would be counted in Silver Gate's restaurant rate.
Silver Gate is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3077125: Virginia City levies a 4% resort tax from April through October on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
3079525: West Yellowstone's resort tax is 4% on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (3% since 1986 and 1% more for infrastructure, approved in 2019; Town of West Yellowstone); it would be counted in West Yellowstone's restaurant rate.
West Yellowstone is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3079825: Whitefish's 3% resort tax on lodging, restaurant and prepared food, alcoholic drinks, ski resort goods and services and luxuries (approved in 1995 and extended by voters in 2021 to January 31, 2045) is counted in Whitefish's restaurant rate (City of Whitefish).

The Big Mountain Resort Area District around Whitefish Mountain Resort, outside the city, levies a 3% resort tax from June 1, 2025, for 20 years (Flathead County's special election of January 21, 2025; approved by 80 of 90 ballots, as reported by NBC Montana; the Department of Commerce's map shows its rate as yet to be set); not counted here, since the district isn't a Census place.
3081400: The Wolf Creek resort area levies a 3% resort tax from April 1 to November 15 on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
30009: The Red Lodge Mountain resort area, the ski area west of the city, has levied a 2% resort tax since January 1, 2008 (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since the area isn't a Census place.
30029: The Big Mountain Resort Area District around Whitefish Mountain Resort, outside the city, levies a 3% resort tax from June 1, 2025, for 20 years (Flathead County's special election of January 21, 2025; approved by 80 of 90 ballots, as reported by NBC Montana; the Department of Commerce's map shows its rate as yet to be set); not counted here, since the district isn't a Census place.

programs: Tax increment financing districts (urban renewal, targeted economic development, industrial and technology districts) are mapped statewide from the Department of Revenue's layer (updated November 2025), each named with its city or county; three it still lists as existing ended July 1, 2026 (Missoula's Technology District and Kalispell's Old School Technology G and Industrial H districts) and are left out. Business improvement districts are mapped from city and county layers in Great Falls, Livingston, Missoula, Helena, Kalispell and Bozeman (the city's base layer); Billings' isn't mapped (no layer found). Communities in the Department of Commerce's Main Street Montana Program are named on their pages.

warn.text: Bozeman draws many visitors (Montana State University, Bridger Bowl and travelers bound for Big Sky and Yellowstone National Park), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (1.6%) and its 70 lodging places (1.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 2 of its 13 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Bozeman is an affiliate community of the Department of Commerce's Main Street Montana Program; its downtown isn't mapped.
Downtown Bozeman's business improvement district isn't mapped: the city publishes no layer of it.

warn.text: Livingston draws many visitors (Paradise Valley and the road to Yellowstone National Park), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (0.6%) and its 18 lodging places (1.9 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though one of its 2 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Livingston is an affiliate community of the Department of Commerce's Main Street Montana Program; its downtown isn't mapped.

warn.text: Kalispell draws many visitors (Flathead Lake and travelers bound for Glacier National Park), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (2.5%) and its 25 lodging places (1.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 2 of its 7 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

warn.text: Gallatin County draws many visitors (Big Sky, West Yellowstone and Bozeman), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the county as a whole: its seasonal homes (5.4%) and its 181 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 4 of its 26 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Helena Valley Northeast's page is built from the census tract it shares with Craig, Wolf Creek and York along the Missouri River, whose cabins and fishing lodging (584 of 1,970 homes seasonal, 29.6%; 10 lodging places) make the tract a visitor economy more than Helena Valley Northeast, which has only 51 of its 126 census blocks in it, so read that flag with care.

Pryor's page is built from the census tract it shares with Fort Smith and St. Xavier, whose fishing lodges on the Bighorn River and cabins by Bighorn Canyon (132 of 593 homes seasonal, 22.3%; 12 lodging places) make the tract a visitor economy more than Pryor itself, so read that flag with care.

St. Xavier's page is built from the census tract it shares with Fort Smith and Pryor, whose fishing lodges on the Bighorn River and cabins by Bighorn Canyon (132 of 593 homes seasonal, 22.3%; 12 lodging places) make the tract a visitor economy more than St. Xavier itself, so read that flag with care.

Superior's flag as a visitor economy rests on the lodging in the census tract it shares with De Borgia, Haugan, Saltese and St. Regis along Interstate 90 (8 lodging places, 3.4 per 1,000 residents; seasonal homes 7.9%, under that cutoff), much of it motels and travel stops serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Glendive's flag as a visitor economy rests on the lodging in its census tract (16 lodging places, 3.6 per 1,000 residents, with few seasonal homes, 2.6%), likely serving travelers on Interstate 94 and oil-field and rail workers more than tourists, so read that flag with care.

programs: Glendive is an affiliate community of the Department of Commerce's Main Street Montana Program; its downtown isn't mapped.

Fairview's flag as a visitor economy rests on the homes the Census counts as seasonal in its census tract (134 of 872, 15.4%, with 2 lodging places), likely housing for oil-field workers or hunting homes more than a tourist trade, so read that flag with care.

Culbertson's flag as a visitor economy rests on the homes the Census counts as seasonal in the census tract it shares with Bainville and Froid (146 of 822, 17.8%, with 3 lodging places), likely housing for oil-field workers or hunting homes more than a tourist trade, so read that flag with care.

Froid's flag as a visitor economy rests on the homes the Census counts as seasonal in the census tract it shares with Bainville and Culbertson (146 of 822, 17.8%, with 3 lodging places), likely housing for oil-field workers or hunting homes more than a tourist trade, so read that flag with care.

Bainville's flag as a visitor economy rests on the homes the Census counts as seasonal in the census tract it shares with Culbertson and Froid (146 of 822, 17.8%, with 3 lodging places), likely housing for oil-field workers or hunting homes more than a tourist trade, so read that flag with care.

Richey's flag as a visitor economy rests on the homes the Census counts as seasonal in the large census tract it shares with Bloomfield and Lindsay (117 of 769, 15.2%, with no lodging places), likely housing for oil-field workers or hunting homes more than a tourist trade, so read that flag with care.

warn: Shelby's page is built from the census tract of its prison (474 residents, no households), which holds only 2 of Shelby's 299 census blocks; the tract with the other 297, where most of the city's homes and businesses are, is left out because Shelby is just under half of it (297 of its 601 blocks). The figures here describe the prison's tract, not the city.
